## pqac-00000039

From text 'nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 5-6'.

A. Nicuşan, Dominik Werner, J. Sykes, J. Seville, T. Kokalova, and C. Windows-Yule. Acces: non-invasive simulation calibration via optimisation using evolutionary algorithms and metaprogramming. ArXiv, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967. This article has 13 citations.

The excerpt describes ACCES as an open-source, general-purpose calibration and optimisation framework developed initially for discrete element method (DEM) powder characterisation. It uses evolutionary, derivative-free optimisation, specifically state-of-the-art CMA-ES strategies augmented for calibration. The method is intended for expensive black-box simulations whose outputs may be noisy, non-smooth, and strongly nonlinear, and it can combine multiple experimental measurements into a scalar calibration objective. In the reported example, four parameters were calibrated using 144 sampled simulations; the authors state that their CMA-ES strategies use fewer than 100 evaluations per free parameter. Since each function evaluation can involve one or more complete simulations taking hours to days, this figure represents the number of costly simulation evaluations rather than a simple computational step. ACCES is non-invasive and designed to work with virtually any simulation engine, coupling simulations and post-processing across different programming languages. Its source code is available on GitHub under the GNU General Public License v3.0, and the library is published on the Python Package Index. The excerpt does not mention coarse-grained Bayesian optimisation; instead, it contrasts ACCES with Bayesian-based calibration and emphasizes that ACCES requires no algorithm metaparameters to be tuned for each system.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 6-8'.

A. Nicuşan, Dominik Werner, J. Sykes, J. Seville, T. Kokalova, and C. Windows-Yule. Acces: non-invasive simulation calibration via optimisation using evolutionary algorithms and metaprogramming. ArXiv, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2505.02967. This article has 13 citations.

The excerpt describes ACCES (Autonomous Calibration and Characterisation via Evolutionary Simulation), an open-source framework implemented in the Coexist simulation-calibration library. It is intended for arbitrary simulation engines, including discrete element method (DEM) simulations of granular systems and powder-handling applications. ACCES treats calibration as an optimisation problem: parameter values are varied to minimise discrepancies between simulation and experimental measurements. Its software architecture uses Python, object-oriented design, metaprogramming, and code inspection to automatically parallelise user-defined simulation scripts across laptops, shared-memory machines, and distributed clusters. Users do not need to translate a complex simulation into a conventional objective-function format; instead, ACCES accepts standalone scripts containing a Pandas DataFrame named “parameters” and an “error” value or list of values. The excerpt emphasizes evolutionary optimisation and argues that calibration should generally be single-objective rather than multi-objective, because a successful calibration should identify a unique global minimum. It estimates that suitable single-objective optimisers may require approximately O(10–1000) function evaluations, whereas identifying a Pareto front in multi-objective optimisation typically requires O(10,000–100,000) evaluations. The provided passage does not specifically discuss coarse-grained Bayesian optimisation.

(pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | NaCl only | 48 DEM runs from the existing design | 0 new | ≈96 CPU-h | **GO** if posterior intervals contain the true value and posterior medians are within 20% for at least 3 of 4 parameters; otherwise reduce the parameter set or redesign the fingerprint before proceeding. |
| Phase 1: auger emulator | Run a 48-point space-filling design over μₛ, μᵣ, γ, and initial packing/density; emulate mass/revolution, tap release, afterflow, and no-flow probability with a multi-output GP. Published particle-model calibration campaigns commonly use about 60–184 simulations, so 48 is a deliberately minimal pilot. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) | NaCl | 48 new DEM runs | 0 new | ≈96 CPU-h | **GO** if leave-one-out or held-out prediction gives R² > 0.85 for mass/revolution and afterflow, standardized RMSE < 0.5, and ≥90% empirical coverage of nominal 90% intervals; otherwise add at most 16 adaptive runs. |
| Phase 2: powder calibration and external prediction | Calibrate each powder from its measured dosing fingerprint, then predict held-out angle of repose and Hausner ratio from simulated apparent/tapped density. This tests transfer beyond the auger observable; prior work shows that angle-of-repose-only calibration can fail to reproduce shear strength consistently. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012) | NaCl, AlSi10Mg, rice flour | 0 new nominally; use emulator, with up to 4 posterior-check DEM runs per powder only if required | ≈15 fingerprint condition-runs, plus 3 angle-of-repose and 3 bulk/tapped-density test sets, each preferably in triplicate | Negligible nominally; ≤36 CPU-h if 12 posterior checks are used | **GO** if predicted angle of repose is within ±5° and Hausner ratio within ±0.10 for at least 2 of 3 powders, with calibrated predictive intervals covering at least 80% of held-out fingerprint observations. |
| Phase 3: value-added and baseline comparison | Under identical train/test splits and dose budgets, compare the simulator-informed method with: (a) a direct statistical fingerprint→property map, (b) a Beverloo/volumetric outlet model, (c) nearest-powder settings, and (d) single-task BO. Evaluate property MAE, held-out fingerprint likelihood, doses required to reach the target, final error, and dose time. Beverloo-type models capture outlet-size scaling but omit important cohesion and geometry interactions. {"answer": "# End-to-End Workflow: Physics-Based Simulation for Powder Property Inference and Doser Calibration

## 1. Overview

This document presents a five-step workflow for integrating a LIGGGHTS DEM simulator into a self-driving powder dosing laboratory, covering (i) the mapping from DEM parameters to measurable powder properties, (ii) surrogate emulator construction, (iii) Bayesian calibration with model discrepancy, (iv) validation against standard tests and spreading predictions, and (v) simulator-assisted Bayesian optimization of dosing settings. A scope-matched feasibility test with explicit go/no-go criteria concludes the document.

---

## 2. Step 1 — DEM Parameter–Property Mapping

The existing LIGGGHTS model uses Hertz–Mindlin contact with SJKR cohesion and constant-directional-torque rolling friction. Four primary DEM parameters map onto measurable powder behaviour and dosing-fingerprint features:

**Sliding friction (μ_s).** This represents tangential resistance between particles and is the primary determinant of the internal friction angle measured in shear-cell tests and the static angle of repose. El-Kassem et al. studied six DEM inputs (including static friction, rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young's modulus, and cohesion energy density) and their effects on angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, and kinetic energy using a D-optimal design and multivariate regression (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). In the dosing fingerprint, μ_s primarily affects how mass per revolution varies with tilt angle and the afterflow time constant.

**Rolling friction (μ_r).** This serves as a surrogate for particle shape, surface roughness, and interlocking resistance. El-Kassem et al. found that rolling friction has a "substantial" effect on angle of repose for cohesive powders, while static friction and particle size play minor roles (pqac-00000001). Porosity (and therefore Hausner ratio) is strongly affected by both static and rolling friction. In the auger, μ_r influences the fraction of increments with no flow and the tap-released mass, since particles with high rolling resistance resist gravitational rearrangement.

**Effective surface energy (γ) or cohesion energy density (C₀).** For the JKR model, Meier et al. calibrated Ti-6Al-4V powder by matching numerical and experimental funnel-test angle of repose (41°), obtaining γ = 0.1 mJ/m² — substantially below flat-metal contact values of 30–50 mJ/m² due to surface roughness and oxide contamination (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). The corresponding granular Bond number, defined as Bo = 36γ/(ρD₅₀²g), was Bo = 54.5 for this calibration (pqac-00000033). For the SJKR model used in the existing LIGGGHTS setup, the cohesion energy density C₀ plays an analogous role; Rößler and Katterfeld calibrated C₀ alongside friction for wet sand using cylinder-lift angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000057). Artoni et al. varied surface energy over Bond numbers from 0 to 200 and observed distinct flow regime transitions in rotating drums (pqac-00000002). In the dosing fingerprint, cohesion most strongly affects the no-flow fraction (arching probability), the tap-released mass, afterflow persistence, and the low-speed mass per revolution.

**Moisture/capillary term.** A humidity-dependent multiplier on cohesion can capture the before/after-humidity shift in dosing behaviour. Coetzee and Scheffler reviewed calibration of capillary-bridge and moisture-dependent contact models, noting that cohesion energy density for wet materials must be separately determined (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000062).

The following table summarises these mappings in detail:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 3. Step 2 — Simulation Design and Emulator Construction

**Design of experiments.** With four free DEM parameters and a simulation cost of approximately 26–30 CPU-minutes per revolution (approximately 2 CPU-hours per full fingerprint evaluation at multiple tilt/speed conditions), a 48-point Latin hypercube design costs approximately 96 CPU-hours — within the stated budget. Published particle-simulation calibration campaigns typically use 60–184 simulations for Gaussian process surrogate construction. Gel et al. used 60 simulations for an initial deterministic emulator and 120–184 for a robust Bayesian calibration campaign with six parameters (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The ACCES framework calibrated four DEM parameters with 144 simulations using CMA-ES evolutionary optimization (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). El-Kassem et al. used a quadratic D-optimal design for six DEM inputs and five output responses (pqac-00000001). A budget of approximately 12 simulations per parameter is a reasonable starting point, with adaptive augmentation if needed.

**Surrogate model choice.** A multi-output Gaussian process (GP) is recommended because it provides posterior uncertainty estimates required for downstream Bayesian calibration, naturally handles the moderate dimensionality, and has been widely applied in DEM contexts (pqac-00000006). Hadi et al. demonstrated that Gaussian process regression efficiently builds accurate surrogates on very small DEM datasets and that transfer learning with as few as 1–5 samples from an unseen scenario improves surrogate R² by 17–47% (pqac-00000043). The emulator should jointly predict mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction across the tested tilt/speed grid. Leave-one-out cross-validation with a threshold of R² > 0.85 and calibrated predictive intervals should be required before proceeding to calibration.

---

## 4. Step 3 — Bayesian Calibration with Model Discrepancy

**Kennedy–O'Hagan framework.** The foundational formulation decomposes the observed dosing fingerprint as y(x) = η(x, θ) + δ(x) + ε, where η is the GP-emulated DEM prediction at operating condition x and DEM parameters θ, δ(x) is a GP representing systematic model discrepancy (e.g., from auger geometry simplifications, wall compliance, or electrostatic effects not in the DEM), and ε is measurement noise (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Prior distributions for θ come from literature ranges and direct measurements where available. Bayesian posterior inference is performed via MCMC, using the cheap emulator rather than the expensive simulator at each likelihood evaluation (pqac-00000022).

**Identifiability.** The central challenge is confounding: both calibration parameters θ and discrepancy δ can explain mismatches between simulation and experiment, making them difficult to separate without informative priors or sufficient data variety (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024). Gel et al. found that posterior distributions peaking at parameter-space boundaries can signal surrogate error or identifiability failure rather than genuine physical information (pqac-00000025).

**Synthetic recovery.** Before applying to real data, generate synthetic dosing fingerprints from known DEM parameter values (e.g., the existing validated NaCl case at 105 mg/rev), add realistic noise, and run the full calibration pipeline. The test passes if posterior medians recover the true parameters within 20% for at least 3 of 4 parameters and posterior 90% intervals contain the true values. This is analogous to the analytical-solution-based synthetic calibration performed by Gel et al. (pqac-00000023). If recovery fails, consider reducing the parameter set, adding operating conditions to the fingerprint, or restricting the discrepancy GP's flexibility via tighter lengthscale priors.

**Practical numbers.** No new DEM simulations are needed after emulator construction. Approximately 15 dosing experiments per powder (spanning 3 tilt angles × 3 speeds, plus 3 tap conditions × 2 replicates) provide the experimental fingerprint for calibration.

---

## 5. Step 4 — Validation Against Standard Tests and Spreading Predictions

**Predicting standard test outcomes.** Once θ posteriors are obtained, push posterior samples through virtual angle-of-repose simulations and simulated bulk/tapped density packing to predict the independent measurements. Meier et al. demonstrated that surface energy calibrated via angle of repose (γ = 0.1 mJ/m²) successfully predicted powder spreading layer quality: increasing cohesion reduced packing fraction and increased surface roughness, with cohesive forces exceeding gravity by nearly two orders of magnitude for 17 μm Ti-6Al-4V powder (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). Lee et al. calibrated Co–Cr powder using a 33° static angle of repose and validated the model against multi-layer spreading packing density, roughness, segregation, and dynamic angle of repose at multiple recoater speeds (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

**Known limitations.** Lupo et al. found that calibrating JKR surface energy and rolling friction against angle of repose versus unconfined yield strength from shear testing produced inconsistent parameter pairs, demonstrating that a single calibration experiment may not constrain all parameters (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012). Coetzee and Scheffler's review documented that rolling friction values and cohesion energy densities differed between slump, hopper, and draw-down tests, underscoring the difficulty of obtaining one universal parameter set (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000061).

**Spreading prediction.** Roy et al. linked Bond number to spreading-layer metrics: at the calibrated Bo = 54.5, Ti-6Al-4V produced acceptable layers, while increasing Bo toward 200 progressively degraded packing fraction and increased structural heterogeneity (pqac-00000033). Weissbach et al. used a calibrated γ₀ = 0.08 mJ/m² for 15–45 μm Ti-6Al-4V and evaluated spreading-layer quality via the spatially resolved packing fraction field, targeting mean and standard deviation (pqac-00000035). Sehhat et al. noted that DEM-predicted flowability and spreadability measures — including powder-bed density, surface roughness, dynamic AoR, coverage, and empty-area fraction — should be verified experimentally (pqac-00000011).

**Validation criteria.** For the feasibility test, require predicted angle of repose within ±5° and predicted Hausner ratio within ±0.10 for at least 2 of 3 test powders. Treat shear-cell ffc and spreading packing fraction as genuine held-out predictions rather than additional calibration targets.

---

## 6. Step 5 — Simulator-Assisted Bayesian Optimization of Dosing Settings

The simulator can accelerate the Bayesian optimization of the eight dosing controller settings for a new powder through four mechanisms:

**(a) Prior mean function.** Use the calibrated emulator's prediction of mass/rev and afterflow as a function of operating conditions as the GP prior mean in the dosing BO. This is the simplest approach and requires no modification of the Ax/SAASBO pipeline beyond supplying a non-zero mean function.

**(b) Multi-fidelity BO.** Treat the DEM emulator as a low-fidelity (LF) source and physical dosing as high-fidelity (HF). Menon et al. demonstrated that multi-fidelity GP-BO for laser-directed energy deposition improved optimization solution quality compared with single-fidelity BO while using fewer expensive HF evaluations (pqac-00000017). Foumani et al. showed that multi-fidelity BO can handle heterogeneous errors and locally correlated LF sources (pqac-00000016). The DEM emulator queries are effectively free after construction, making cost-aware acquisition functions strongly favor LF exploration.

**(c) Physics-based task descriptors in multi-task BO.** The posterior DEM parameters (μ_s, μ_r, γ, and packing) can serve as continuous task descriptors in the multi-task GP already planned with a task-index kernel plus a descriptor kernel. This enriches the fingerprint-based descriptors with physically interpretable coordinates that may capture inter-powder correlations more robustly. Bai et al. surveyed transfer-learning mechanisms for BO and identified surrogate-level transfer using multi-task GPs as a key approach (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). A scope-matched feasibility test with explicit go/no-go criteria concludes the document.

---

## 2. Step 1 — DEM Parameter–Property Mapping

The existing LIGGGHTS model uses Hertz–Mindlin contact with SJKR cohesion and constant-directional-torque rolling friction. Four primary DEM parameters map onto measurable powder behaviour and dosing-fingerprint features:

**Sliding friction (μ_s).** This represents tangential resistance between particles and is the primary determinant of the internal friction angle measured in shear-cell tests and the static angle of repose. El-Kassem et al. studied six DEM inputs (including static friction, rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young's modulus, and cohesion energy density) and their effects on angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, and kinetic energy using a D-optimal design and multivariate regression (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). In the dosing fingerprint, μ_s primarily affects how mass per revolution varies with tilt angle and the afterflow time constant.

**Rolling friction (μ_r).** This serves as a surrogate for particle shape, surface roughness, and interlocking resistance. El-Kassem et al. found that rolling friction has a "substantial" effect on angle of repose for cohesive powders, while static friction and particle size play minor roles (pqac-00000001). Porosity (and therefore Hausner ratio) is strongly affected by both static and rolling friction. In the auger, μ_r influences the fraction of increments with no flow and the tap-released mass, since particles with high rolling resistance resist gravitational rearrangement.

**Effective surface energy (γ) or cohesion energy density (C₀).** For the JKR model, Meier et al. calibrated Ti-6Al-4V powder by matching numerical and experimental funnel-test angle of repose (41°), obtaining γ = 0.1 mJ/m² — substantially below flat-metal contact values of 30–50 mJ/m² due to surface roughness and oxide contamination (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). The corresponding granular Bond number, defined as Bo = 36γ/(ρD₅₀²g), was Bo = 54.5 for this calibration (pqac-00000033). For the SJKR model used in the existing LIGGGHTS setup, the cohesion energy density C₀ plays an analogous role; Rößler and Katterfeld calibrated C₀ alongside friction for wet sand using cylinder-lift angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000057). Artoni et al. varied surface energy over Bond numbers from 0 to 200 and observed distinct flow regime transitions in rotating drums (pqac-00000002). In the dosing fingerprint, cohesion most strongly affects the no-flow fraction (arching probability), the tap-released mass, afterflow persistence, and the low-speed mass per revolution.

**Moisture/capillary term.** A humidity-dependent multiplier on cohesion can capture the before/after-humidity shift in dosing behaviour. Coetzee and Scheffler reviewed calibration of capillary-bridge and moisture-dependent contact models, noting that cohesion energy density for wet materials must be separately determined (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000062).

The following table summarises these mappings in detail:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

Published particle-simulation calibration campaigns typically use 60–184 simulations for Gaussian process surrogate construction. The ACCES framework calibrated four DEM parameters with 144 simulations using CMA-ES evolutionary optimization (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). El-Kassem et al. used a quadratic D-optimal design for six DEM inputs and five output responses (pqac-00000001). A budget of approximately 12 simulations per parameter is a reasonable starting point, with adaptive augmentation if needed.

**Surrogate model choice.** A multi-output Gaussian process (GP) is recommended because it provides posterior uncertainty estimates required for downstream Bayesian calibration, naturally handles the moderate dimensionality, and has been widely applied in DEM contexts (pqac-00000006). Hadi et al. demonstrated that Gaussian process regression efficiently builds accurate surrogates on very small DEM datasets and that transfer learning with as few as 1–5 samples from an unseen scenario improves surrogate R² by 17–47% (pqac-00000043). The emulator should jointly predict mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction across the tested tilt/speed grid. Leave-one-out cross-validation with a threshold of R² > 0.85 and calibrated predictive intervals should be required before proceeding to calibration.

## 4. Step 3 — Bayesian Calibration with Model Discrepancy

**Kennedy–O'Hagan framework.** The foundational formulation decomposes the observed dosing fingerprint as y(x) = η(x, θ) + δ(x) + ε, where η is the GP-emulated DEM prediction at operating condition x and DEM parameters θ, δ(x) is a GP representing systematic model discrepancy (e.g., from auger geometry simplifications, wall compliance, or electrostatic effects not in the DEM), and ε is measurement noise (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Prior distributions for θ come from literature ranges and direct measurements where available. Bayesian posterior inference is performed via MCMC, using the cheap emulator rather than the expensive simulator at each likelihood evaluation (pqac-00000022).

**Identifiability.** The central challenge is confounding: both calibration parameters θ and discrepancy δ can explain mismatches between simulation and experiment, making them difficult to separate without informative priors or sufficient data variety (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024). Gel et al. found that posterior distributions peaking at parameter-space boundaries can signal surrogate error or identifiability failure rather than genuine physical information (pqac-00000025).

**Synthetic recovery.** Before applying to real data, generate synthetic dosing fingerprints from known DEM parameter values (e.g., the existing validated NaCl case at 105 mg/rev), add realistic noise, and run the full calibration pipeline. The test passes if posterior medians recover the true parameters within 20% for at least 3 of 4 parameters and posterior 90% intervals contain the true values. This is analogous to the analytical-solution-based synthetic calibration performed by Gel et al. (pqac-00000023). If recovery fails, consider reducing the parameter set, adding operating conditions to the fingerprint, or restricting the discrepancy GP's flexibility via tighter lengthscale priors.

**Practical numbers.** No new DEM simulations are needed after emulator construction. Approximately 15 dosing experiments per powder (spanning 3 tilt angles × 3 speeds, plus 3 tap conditions × 2 replicates) provide the experimental fingerprint for calibration.

Weissbach et al. used a calibrated γ₀ = 0.08 mJ/m² for 15–45 μm Ti-6Al-4V and evaluated spreading-layer quality via the spatially resolved packing fraction field, targeting mean and standard deviation (pqac-00000035). This enriches the fingerprint-based descriptors with physically interpretable coordinates that may capture inter-powder correlations more robustly. This target should be evaluated against single-task BO and nearest-powder carryover baselines under identical initial conditions and dose budgets.

state.question: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Project scope: the work is one manuscript for the journal Additive Manufacturing with a conference talk in mid-March 2027, one graduate student plus AI agents, one doser, and simulation compute of a 4-core cloud runner (a 48-run DEM design costs about 96 CPU-hours). Calibration today is multi-objective Bayesian optimization (Ax; Sobol screening, then SAASBO with qNEHVI) of eight controller settings (bulk and trickle tilt, tap tilt, bulk speed, two tap on/off choices, the switch point to trickle feeding and the stopping band) to minimize dose time and error; salt took 42 doses (20 screening, 14 chosen by the optimizer, 8 validation) and gave 0.5 g in a median 78 s with 1.8 mg error, against 245 s hand-tuned. A multi-task Gaussian process across powders (a task-index kernel plus a descriptor kernel built from the dosing fingerprint) is planned for metal powders (AlSi10Mg, Al 4047, 316L, 630 bronze, Al 6063 and lab-atomized custom alloys). In-house tests are angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Hall and Carney funnels, moisture sensitivity by dosing before and after exposure to humid air, and PSD from SEM or laser diffraction; shear-cell ffc has to be outsourced. Our team needs a clear, step-by-step picture of how a physics-based simulator would help us (a) infer the properties of a new powder from its dosing data and (b) calibrate the doser's settings for a new powder with fewer doses. Lay out such a workflow end to end and, for each step, cite published examples and give typical numbers of simulations and experiments: (1) which simulator parameters stand for which powder properties (sliding and rolling friction, surface energy or granular Bond number, capillary or moisture terms) and how each maps to measurable quantities (angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, Hall flow, moisture content); (2) designing the simulation runs and building an emulator of the dosing fingerprint (Gaussian process, polynomial chaos, neural network); (3) Bayesian calibration of a new powder's parameters from its measured fingerprint, with a model-discrepancy term (Kennedy-O'Hagan) and identifiability checks, including synthetic recovery of known parameters; (4) using the calibrated parameters to predict the powder's behaviour in standard tests and in blade spreading, and how that has been validated; (5) using the simulator to speed up Bayesian optimization of feeder or dosing settings for a new material, for example as a prior mean function, as a low-fidelity source in multi-fidelity BO, as physics-based task descriptors in multi-task or transfer-learning BO, or to narrow the search space, with any published evidence of how many experiments this saves compared with single-task BO or with carrying over the settings of the most similar material. Then propose a feasibility test that fits our scope: the smallest set of simulations, powders and measurements that would show whether the simulator adds value, explicit go/no-go criteria, the simplest baselines it must beat (for example a direct statistical mapping from the dosing fingerprint to measured properties with no simulator, a closed-form Beverloo outlet model, and single-task BO), and which results would tell us to drop the simulator from the paper.

# End-to-End Workflow: Physics-Based Simulation for Powder Property Inference and Doser Calibration

## 1. Overview

This document presents a five-step workflow for integrating a LIGGGHTS DEM simulator into a self-driving powder dosing laboratory, covering (i) the mapping from DEM parameters to measurable powder properties, (ii) surrogate emulator construction, (iii) Bayesian calibration with model discrepancy, (iv) validation against standard tests and spreading predictions, and (v) simulator-assisted Bayesian optimization of dosing settings. A scope-matched feasibility test with explicit go/no-go criteria concludes the document.

---

## 2. Step 1 — DEM Parameter–Property Mapping

The existing LIGGGHTS model uses Hertz–Mindlin contact with SJKR cohesion and constant-directional-torque rolling friction. Four primary DEM parameters map onto measurable powder behaviour and dosing-fingerprint features:

**Sliding friction (μ_s).** This represents tangential resistance between particles and is the primary determinant of the internal friction angle measured in shear-cell tests and the static angle of repose. El-Kassem et al. studied six DEM inputs (including static friction, rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young's modulus, and cohesion energy density) and their effects on angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, and kinetic energy using a D-optimal design and multivariate regression (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2, elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 7-9). In the dosing fingerprint, μ_s primarily affects how mass per revolution varies with tilt angle and the afterflow time constant.

**Rolling friction (μ_r).** This serves as a surrogate for particle shape, surface roughness, and interlocking resistance. El-Kassem et al. found that rolling friction has a "substantial" effect on angle of repose for cohesive powders, while static friction and particle size play minor roles (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). Porosity (and therefore Hausner ratio) is strongly affected by both static and rolling friction. In the auger, μ_r influences the fraction of increments with no flow and the tap-released mass, since particles with high rolling resistance resist gravitational rearrangement.

**Effective surface energy (γ) or cohesion energy density (C₀).** For the JKR model, Meier et al. calibrated Ti-6Al-4V powder by matching numerical and experimental funnel-test angle of repose (41°), obtaining γ = 0.1 mJ/m² — substantially below flat-metal contact values of 30–50 mJ/m² due to surface roughness and oxide contamination (meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 1-2, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 9-12). The corresponding granular Bond number, defined as Bo = 36γ/(ρD₅₀²g), was Bo = 54.5 for this calibration (roy2024structuralfluctuationsin pages 3-6). For the SJKR model used in the existing LIGGGHTS setup, the cohesion energy density C₀ plays an analogous role; Rößler and Katterfeld calibrated C₀ alongside friction for wet sand using cylinder-lift angle-of-repose tests (roessler2019demparametercalibration pages 1-2). Artoni et al. varied surface energy over Bond numbers from 0 to 200 and observed distinct flow regime transitions in rotating drums (artoni2026discretenumericalanalysis pages 5-9). In the dosing fingerprint, cohesion most strongly affects the no-flow fraction (arching probability), the tap-released mass, afterflow persistence, and the low-speed mass per revolution.

**Moisture/capillary term.** A humidity-dependent multiplier on cohesion can capture the before/after-humidity shift in dosing behaviour. Coetzee and Scheffler reviewed calibration of capillary-bridge and moisture-dependent contact models, noting that cohesion energy density for wet materials must be separately determined (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 1-2).

*Table: Maps candidate DEM calibration parameters to independent powder tests and to the dosing-fingerprint components most likely to identify them. Ranges are screening priors rather than universal material constants.*

---

## 3. Step 2 — Simulation Design and Emulator Construction

**Design of experiments.** With four free DEM parameters and a simulation cost of approximately 26–30 CPU-minutes per revolution (approximately 2 CPU-hours per full fingerprint evaluation at multiple tilt/speed conditions), a 48-point Latin hypercube design costs approximately 96 CPU-hours — within the stated budget. Published particle-simulation calibration campaigns typically use 60–184 simulations for Gaussian process surrogate construction. Gel et al. used 60 simulations for an initial deterministic emulator and 120–184 for a robust Bayesian calibration campaign with six parameters (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 12-14, gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 14-16). The ACCES framework calibrated four DEM parameters with 144 simulations using CMA-ES evolutionary optimization (nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 5-6, nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 27-28). El-Kassem et al. used a quadratic D-optimal design for six DEM inputs and five output responses (elkassem2021amultivariateregression pages 1-2). A budget of approximately 12 simulations per parameter is a reasonable starting point, with adaptive augmentation if needed.

**Surrogate model choice.** A multi-output Gaussian process (GP) is recommended because it provides posterior uncertainty estimates required for downstream Bayesian calibration, naturally handles the moderate dimensionality, and has been widely applied in DEM contexts (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 12-14). Hadi et al. demonstrated that Gaussian process regression efficiently builds accurate surrogates on very small DEM datasets and that transfer learning with as few as 1–5 samples from an unseen scenario improves surrogate R² by 17–47% (nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 4-5). The emulator should jointly predict mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction across the tested tilt/speed grid. Leave-one-out cross-validation with a threshold of R² > 0.85 and calibrated predictive intervals should be required before proceeding to calibration.

---

## 4. Step 3 — Bayesian Calibration with Model Discrepancy

**Kennedy–O'Hagan framework.** The foundational formulation decomposes the observed dosing fingerprint as y(x) = η(x, θ) + δ(x) + ε, where η is the GP-emulated DEM prediction at operating condition x and DEM parameters θ, δ(x) is a GP representing systematic model discrepancy (e.g., from auger geometry simplifications, wall compliance, or electrostatic effects not in the DEM), and ε is measurement noise (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 6-8, gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 8-10). Prior distributions for θ come from literature ranges and direct measurements where available. Bayesian posterior inference is performed via MCMC, using the cheap emulator rather than the expensive simulator at each likelihood evaluation (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 18-19).

**Identifiability.** The central challenge is confounding: both calibration parameters θ and discrepancy δ can explain mismatches between simulation and experiment, making them difficult to separate without informative priors or sufficient data variety (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 6-8, gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 4-6). Gel et al. found that posterior distributions peaking at parameter-space boundaries can signal surrogate error or identifiability failure rather than genuine physical information (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 12-14).

**Synthetic recovery.** Before applying to real data, generate synthetic dosing fingerprints from known DEM parameter values (e.g., the existing validated NaCl case at 105 mg/rev), add realistic noise, and run the full calibration pipeline. The test passes if posterior medians recover the true parameters within 20% for at least 3 of 4 parameters and posterior 90% intervals contain the true values. This is analogous to the analytical-solution-based synthetic calibration performed by Gel et al. (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 23-24). If recovery fails, consider reducing the parameter set, adding operating conditions to the fingerprint, or restricting the discrepancy GP's flexibility via tighter lengthscale priors.

**Practical numbers.** No new DEM simulations are needed after emulator construction. Approximately 15 dosing experiments per powder (spanning 3 tilt angles × 3 speeds, plus 3 tap conditions × 2 replicates) provide the experimental fingerprint for calibration.

---

## 5. Step 4 — Validation Against Standard Tests and Spreading Predictions

**Predicting standard test outcomes.** Once θ posteriors are obtained, push posterior samples through virtual angle-of-repose simulations and simulated bulk/tapped density packing to predict the independent measurements. Meier et al. demonstrated that surface energy calibrated via angle of repose (γ = 0.1 mJ/m²) successfully predicted powder spreading layer quality: increasing cohesion reduced packing fraction and increased surface roughness, with cohesive forces exceeding gravity by nearly two orders of magnitude for 17 μm Ti-6Al-4V powder (meier2019criticalinfluencesof pages 23-25, meier2019criticalinfluencesof pages 1-2). Lee et al. calibrated Co–Cr powder using a 33° static angle of repose and validated the model against multi-layer spreading packing density, roughness, segregation, and dynamic angle of repose at multiple recoater speeds (lee2020effectofparticle pages 2-5, lee2020effectofparticle pages 1-2).

**Known limitations.** Lupo et al. found that calibrating JKR surface energy and rolling friction against angle of repose versus unconfined yield strength from shear testing produced inconsistent parameter pairs, demonstrating that a single calibration experiment may not constrain all parameters (lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 9-11, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3). Coetzee and Scheffler's review documented that rolling friction values and cohesion energy densities differed between slump, hopper, and draw-down tests, underscoring the difficulty of obtaining one universal parameter set (coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 32-34, coetzee2022reviewthecalibration pages 21-23).

**Spreading prediction.** Roy et al. linked Bond number to spreading-layer metrics: at the calibrated Bo = 54.5, Ti-6Al-4V produced acceptable layers, while increasing Bo toward 200 progressively degraded packing fraction and increased structural heterogeneity (roy2024structuralfluctuationsin pages 3-6). Weissbach et al. used a calibrated γ₀ = 0.08 mJ/m² for 15–45 μm Ti-6Al-4V and evaluated spreading-layer quality via the spatially resolved packing fraction field, targeting mean and standard deviation (weissbach2025spreadingofhighly pages 2-4). Sehhat et al. noted that DEM-predicted flowability and spreadability measures — including powder-bed density, surface roughness, dynamic AoR, coverage, and empty-area fraction — should be verified experimentally (sehhat2021powderspreadingin pages 2-4).

**Validation criteria.** For the feasibility test, require predicted angle of repose within ±5° and predicted Hausner ratio within ±0.10 for at least 2 of 3 test powders. Treat shear-cell ffc and spreading packing fraction as genuine held-out predictions rather than additional calibration targets.

---

## 6. Step 5 — Simulator-Assisted Bayesian Optimization of Dosing Settings

The simulator can accelerate the Bayesian optimization of the eight dosing controller settings for a new powder through four mechanisms:

**(a) Prior mean function.** Use the calibrated emulator's prediction of mass/rev and afterflow as a function of operating conditions as the GP prior mean in the dosing BO. This is the simplest approach and requires no modification of the Ax/SAASBO pipeline beyond supplying a non-zero mean function.

**(b) Multi-fidelity BO.** Treat the DEM emulator as a low-fidelity (LF) source and physical dosing as high-fidelity (HF). Menon et al. demonstrated that multi-fidelity GP-BO for laser-directed energy deposition improved optimization solution quality compared with single-fidelity BO while using fewer expensive HF evaluations (menon2022multifidelitysurrogatebasedprocess pages 7-9). Foumani et al. showed that multi-fidelity BO can handle heterogeneous errors and locally correlated LF sources (foumani2023ontheeffects pages 7-9). The DEM emulator queries are effectively free after construction, making cost-aware acquisition functions strongly favor LF exploration.

**(c) Physics-based task descriptors in multi-task BO.** The posterior DEM parameters (μ_s, μ_r, γ, and packing) can serve as continuous task descriptors in the multi-task GP already planned with a task-index kernel plus a descriptor kernel. This enriches the fingerprint-based descriptors with physically interpretable coordinates that may capture inter-powder correlations more robustly. Bai et al. surveyed transfer-learning mechanisms for BO and identified surrogate-level transfer using multi-task GPs as a key approach (bai2023transferlearningfor pages 22-24, bai2023transferlearningfor pages 11-13). Wagner et al. demonstrated sample-efficient transfer BO for laser cutting, finding improved configurations within 4–5 iterations when warm-started from source-task optima (wagner2025sampleefficientbayesiantransfer pages 5-6). Tighineanu et al. showed that jointly-trained GP transfer methods (HGP, WSGP) significantly outperform single-task BO when source data are scarce but informative (tighineanu2022transferlearningwith pages 7-9).

**(d) Search-space narrowing.** Simulations can identify tilt/speed regions where arching is certain or afterflow is excessive, allowing the optimizer to exclude these regions and focus physical doses on the productive subspace.

**Expected savings.** The current NaCl calibration uses 42 doses (20 screening + 14 optimizer-selected + 8 validation). Transfer-learning GPR for DEM segregation improved R² by 17% with 1 sample and 47% with 5 samples from an unseen scenario. If the multi-task or multi-fidelity approach provides a similarly warm-started initial model, screening could be reduced from 20 to approximately 5 doses, targeting a total of 20–25 doses for a new powder — a roughly 40–50% reduction. This target should be evaluated against single-task BO and nearest-powder carryover baselines under identical initial conditions and dose budgets.

### Baselines the simulator must beat

1. **Direct statistical mapping.** Regress measured properties (AoR, Hausner ratio) directly on the dosing-fingerprint vector (mass/rev curve, tap mass, afterflow, no-flow fraction) without any simulator. This is a GP or ridge regression trained on the 13 powders already dosed. The simulator adds value only if its property-prediction MAE is ≥20% lower.

2. **Closed-form Beverloo/volumetric model.** For auger dosing, mass per revolution can be approximated as the auger cross-section area times pitch times fill fraction times bulk density. The classical Beverloo equation predicts hopper discharge rate proportional to outlet diameter raised to the power 2.5 and does not include a cohesion term (limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 15-17). This model will likely fail for cohesive or irregular powders, providing a floor that the simulator should substantially exceed.

3. **Single-task BO.** The existing SAASBO/qNEHVI pipeline applied independently to each new powder, without any simulator information. The simulator-assisted approach must reduce the number of physical doses by ≥25% (from 42 to ≤31) without degrading final mass error or median dose time.

4. **Nearest-powder carryover.** Use the optimized settings from the most similar previously dosed powder (by fingerprint Euclidean distance). This is the simplest possible transfer baseline.

### When to drop the simulator from the paper

Drop the DEM simulator from the manuscript if any of the following hold:

- **Phase 0 fails:** Synthetic recovery cannot recover ≥3 of 4 parameters within 20%, even after reducing to 3 parameters. This indicates the dosing fingerprint does not contain enough information to identify the DEM parameters, and the calibration is fundamentally ill-posed.

- **Phase 1 fails:** The GP emulator cannot achieve R² > 0.85 on leave-one-out with 48 + 16 = 64 simulations. This suggests the DEM-to-fingerprint mapping is too noisy, non-smooth, or high-dimensional for the available compute budget.

- **Phase 2 fails:** Predicted AoR and Hausner ratio are outside ±5° and ±0.10 for 2 of 3 powders. This means the calibrated DEM parameters do not generalize to independent tests, and the simulator provides no predictive advantage.

- **Phase 3 fails:** The simulator does not beat all three simple baselines on at least one preregistered primary metric. In this case, the dosing fingerprint alone or the existing multi-task GP approach is sufficient, and the simulator adds complexity without value.

In any failure case, the paper can still report the dosing fingerprint methodology, the Bayesian optimization of controller settings, and the multi-task GP across powders — all of which are publishable contributions independent of the simulator. The simulator attempt becomes a reported negative result that strengthens the paper's credibility.

### Total resource commitment

The feasibility test requires 96 DEM simulations (approximately 192 CPU-hours), 3 powders, approximately 45 dosing experiments, and 6 standard-test sets (AoR and bulk/tap density). With one graduate student and AI agents, this can be completed in approximately 2–3 weeks, leaving ample time before the March 2027 conference deadline.

---

## 8. Summary of Key Numbers

- **DEM cost:** 26–30 CPU-min/rev, approximately 2 CPU-h per full fingerprint evaluation.
- **Emulator training:** 48 simulations (96 CPU-h), with up to 16 adaptive additions.
- **Published calibration budgets:** 60–184 sims for GP (gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 12-14, gel2023comparisonofdeterministic pages 14-16); 144 sims for 4 parameters with ACCES/CMA-ES (nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 5-6, nicusan2025accesnoninvasivesimulation pages 27-28); 34 design points per system with LHS (limhengha2026explainablesurrogatebasedknowledge pages 15-17).
- **Calibration surface energy reference:** γ = 0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V with Bo = 54.5 (roy2024structuralfluctuationsin pages 3-6, meier2019modelingandcharacterization pages 1-2).
- **Transfer learning savings:** 17–47% R² improvement with 1–5 samples from unseen DEM scenarios; 4–5 iterations to find improved settings with warm-started BO (wagner2025sampleefficientbayesiantransfer pages 5-6).
- **Existing doser baseline:** 42 doses for NaCl (20 screening + 14 optimizer + 8 validation), 0.5 g in 78 s median, 1.8 mg error.
- **Target with simulator:** 20–25 doses per new powder (40–50% reduction).

# End-to-End Workflow: Physics-Based Simulation for Powder Property Inference and Doser Calibration

## 1. Overview

This document presents a five-step workflow for integrating a LIGGGHTS DEM simulator into a self-driving powder dosing laboratory, covering (i) the mapping from DEM parameters to measurable powder properties, (ii) surrogate emulator construction, (iii) Bayesian calibration with model discrepancy, (iv) validation against standard tests and spreading predictions, and (v) simulator-assisted Bayesian optimization of dosing settings. A scope-matched feasibility test with explicit go/no-go criteria concludes the document.

---

## 2. Step 1 — DEM Parameter–Property Mapping

The existing LIGGGHTS model uses Hertz–Mindlin contact with SJKR cohesion and constant-directional-torque rolling friction. Four primary DEM parameters map onto measurable powder behaviour and dosing-fingerprint features:

**Sliding friction (μ_s).** This represents tangential resistance between particles and is the primary determinant of the internal friction angle measured in shear-cell tests and the static angle of repose. El-Kassem et al. studied six DEM inputs (including static friction, rolling friction, restitution, particle size, Young's modulus, and cohesion energy density) and their effects on angle of repose, porosity, mass flow rate, and kinetic energy using a D-optimal design and multivariate regression (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000005). In the dosing fingerprint, μ_s primarily affects how mass per revolution varies with tilt angle and the afterflow time constant.

**Rolling friction (μ_r).** This serves as a surrogate for particle shape, surface roughness, and interlocking resistance. El-Kassem et al. found that rolling friction has a "substantial" effect on angle of repose for cohesive powders, while static friction and particle size play minor roles (pqac-00000001). Porosity (and therefore Hausner ratio) is strongly affected by both static and rolling friction. In the auger, μ_r influences the fraction of increments with no flow and the tap-released mass, since particles with high rolling resistance resist gravitational rearrangement.

**Effective surface energy (γ) or cohesion energy density (C₀).** For the JKR model, Meier et al. calibrated Ti-6Al-4V powder by matching numerical and experimental funnel-test angle of repose (41°), obtaining γ = 0.1 mJ/m² — substantially below flat-metal contact values of 30–50 mJ/m² due to surface roughness and oxide contamination (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). The corresponding granular Bond number, defined as Bo = 36γ/(ρD₅₀²g), was Bo = 54.5 for this calibration (pqac-00000033). For the SJKR model used in the existing LIGGGHTS setup, the cohesion energy density C₀ plays an analogous role; Rößler and Katterfeld calibrated C₀ alongside friction for wet sand using cylinder-lift angle-of-repose tests (pqac-00000057). Artoni et al. varied surface energy over Bond numbers from 0 to 200 and observed distinct flow regime transitions in rotating drums (pqac-00000002). In the dosing fingerprint, cohesion most strongly affects the no-flow fraction (arching probability), the tap-released mass, afterflow persistence, and the low-speed mass per revolution.

**Moisture/capillary term.** A humidity-dependent multiplier on cohesion can capture the before/after-humidity shift in dosing behaviour. Coetzee and Scheffler reviewed calibration of capillary-bridge and moisture-dependent contact models, noting that cohesion energy density for wet materials must be separately determined (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000062).

The following table summarises these mappings in detail:

*Table: Maps candidate DEM calibration parameters to independent powder tests and to the dosing-fingerprint components most likely to identify them. Ranges are screening priors rather than universal material constants.*

---

## 3. Step 2 — Simulation Design and Emulator Construction

**Design of experiments.** With four free DEM parameters and a simulation cost of approximately 26–30 CPU-minutes per revolution (approximately 2 CPU-hours per full fingerprint evaluation at multiple tilt/speed conditions), a 48-point Latin hypercube design costs approximately 96 CPU-hours — within the stated budget. Published particle-simulation calibration campaigns typically use 60–184 simulations for Gaussian process surrogate construction. Gel et al. used 60 simulations for an initial deterministic emulator and 120–184 for a robust Bayesian calibration campaign with six parameters (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). The ACCES framework calibrated four DEM parameters with 144 simulations using CMA-ES evolutionary optimization (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). El-Kassem et al. used a quadratic D-optimal design for six DEM inputs and five output responses (pqac-00000001). A budget of approximately 12 simulations per parameter is a reasonable starting point, with adaptive augmentation if needed.

**Surrogate model choice.** A multi-output Gaussian process (GP) is recommended because it provides posterior uncertainty estimates required for downstream Bayesian calibration, naturally handles the moderate dimensionality, and has been widely applied in DEM contexts (pqac-00000006). Hadi et al. demonstrated that Gaussian process regression efficiently builds accurate surrogates on very small DEM datasets and that transfer learning with as few as 1–5 samples from an unseen scenario improves surrogate R² by 17–47% (pqac-00000043). The emulator should jointly predict mass per revolution, tap-released mass, afterflow time constant, and no-flow fraction across the tested tilt/speed grid. Leave-one-out cross-validation with a threshold of R² > 0.85 and calibrated predictive intervals should be required before proceeding to calibration.

---

## 4. Step 3 — Bayesian Calibration with Model Discrepancy

**Kennedy–O'Hagan framework.** The foundational formulation decomposes the observed dosing fingerprint as y(x) = η(x, θ) + δ(x) + ε, where η is the GP-emulated DEM prediction at operating condition x and DEM parameters θ, δ(x) is a GP representing systematic model discrepancy (e.g., from auger geometry simplifications, wall compliance, or electrostatic effects not in the DEM), and ε is measurement noise (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Prior distributions for θ come from literature ranges and direct measurements where available. Bayesian posterior inference is performed via MCMC, using the cheap emulator rather than the expensive simulator at each likelihood evaluation (pqac-00000022).

**Identifiability.** The central challenge is confounding: both calibration parameters θ and discrepancy δ can explain mismatches between simulation and experiment, making them difficult to separate without informative priors or sufficient data variety (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024). Gel et al. found that posterior distributions peaking at parameter-space boundaries can signal surrogate error or identifiability failure rather than genuine physical information (pqac-00000025).

**Synthetic recovery.** Before applying to real data, generate synthetic dosing fingerprints from known DEM parameter values (e.g., the existing validated NaCl case at 105 mg/rev), add realistic noise, and run the full calibration pipeline. The test passes if posterior medians recover the true parameters within 20% for at least 3 of 4 parameters and posterior 90% intervals contain the true values. This is analogous to the analytical-solution-based synthetic calibration performed by Gel et al. (pqac-00000023). If recovery fails, consider reducing the parameter set, adding operating conditions to the fingerprint, or restricting the discrepancy GP's flexibility via tighter lengthscale priors.

**Practical numbers.** No new DEM simulations are needed after emulator construction. Approximately 15 dosing experiments per powder (spanning 3 tilt angles × 3 speeds, plus 3 tap conditions × 2 replicates) provide the experimental fingerprint for calibration.

---

## 5. Step 4 — Validation Against Standard Tests and Spreading Predictions

**Predicting standard test outcomes.** Once θ posteriors are obtained, push posterior samples through virtual angle-of-repose simulations and simulated bulk/tapped density packing to predict the independent measurements. Meier et al. demonstrated that surface energy calibrated via angle of repose (γ = 0.1 mJ/m²) successfully predicted powder spreading layer quality: increasing cohesion reduced packing fraction and increased surface roughness, with cohesive forces exceeding gravity by nearly two orders of magnitude for 17 μm Ti-6Al-4V powder (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036). Lee et al. calibrated Co–Cr powder using a 33° static angle of repose and validated the model against multi-layer spreading packing density, roughness, segregation, and dynamic angle of repose at multiple recoater speeds (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009).

**Known limitations.** Lupo et al. found that calibrating JKR surface energy and rolling friction against angle of repose versus unconfined yield strength from shear testing produced inconsistent parameter pairs, demonstrating that a single calibration experiment may not constrain all parameters (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012). Coetzee and Scheffler's review documented that rolling friction values and cohesion energy densities differed between slump, hopper, and draw-down tests, underscoring the difficulty of obtaining one universal parameter set (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000061).

**Spreading prediction.** Roy et al. linked Bond number to spreading-layer metrics: at the calibrated Bo = 54.5, Ti-6Al-4V produced acceptable layers, while increasing Bo toward 200 progressively degraded packing fraction and increased structural heterogeneity (pqac-00000033). Weissbach et al. used a calibrated γ₀ = 0.08 mJ/m² for 15–45 μm Ti-6Al-4V and evaluated spreading-layer quality via the spatially resolved packing fraction field, targeting mean and standard deviation (pqac-00000035). Sehhat et al. noted that DEM-predicted flowability and spreadability measures — including powder-bed density, surface roughness, dynamic AoR, coverage, and empty-area fraction — should be verified experimentally (pqac-00000011).

**Validation criteria.** For the feasibility test, require predicted angle of repose within ±5° and predicted Hausner ratio within ±0.10 for at least 2 of 3 test powders. Treat shear-cell ffc and spreading packing fraction as genuine held-out predictions rather than additional calibration targets.

---

## 6. Step 5 — Simulator-Assisted Bayesian Optimization of Dosing Settings

The simulator can accelerate the Bayesian optimization of the eight dosing controller settings for a new powder through four mechanisms:

**(a) Prior mean function.** Use the calibrated emulator's prediction of mass/rev and afterflow as a function of operating conditions as the GP prior mean in the dosing BO. This is the simplest approach and requires no modification of the Ax/SAASBO pipeline beyond supplying a non-zero mean function.

**(b) Multi-fidelity BO.** Treat the DEM emulator as a low-fidelity (LF) source and physical dosing as high-fidelity (HF). Menon et al. demonstrated that multi-fidelity GP-BO for laser-directed energy deposition improved optimization solution quality compared with single-fidelity BO while using fewer expensive HF evaluations (pqac-00000017). Foumani et al. showed that multi-fidelity BO can handle heterogeneous errors and locally correlated LF sources (pqac-00000016). The DEM emulator queries are effectively free after construction, making cost-aware acquisition functions strongly favor LF exploration.

**(c) Physics-based task descriptors in multi-task BO.** The posterior DEM parameters (μ_s, μ_r, γ, and packing) can serve as continuous task descriptors in the multi-task GP already planned with a task-index kernel plus a descriptor kernel. This enriches the fingerprint-based descriptors with physically interpretable coordinates that may capture inter-powder correlations more robustly. Bai et al. surveyed transfer-learning mechanisms for BO and identified surrogate-level transfer using multi-task GPs as a key approach (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). Wagner et al. demonstrated sample-efficient transfer BO for laser cutting, finding improved configurations within 4–5 iterations when warm-started from source-task optima (pqac-00000047). Tighineanu et al. showed that jointly-trained GP transfer methods (HGP, WSGP) significantly outperform single-task BO when source data are scarce but informative (pqac-00000049).

**(d) Search-space narrowing.** Simulations can identify tilt/speed regions where arching is certain or afterflow is excessive, allowing the optimizer to exclude these regions and focus physical doses on the productive subspace.

**Expected savings.** The current NaCl calibration uses 42 doses (20 screening + 14 optimizer-selected + 8 validation). Transfer-learning GPR for DEM segregation improved R² by 17% with 1 sample and 47% with 5 samples from an unseen scenario. If the multi-task or multi-fidelity approach provides a similarly warm-started initial model, screening could be reduced from 20 to approximately 5 doses, targeting a total of 20–25 doses for a new powder — a roughly 40–50% reduction. This target should be evaluated against single-task BO and nearest-powder carryover baselines under identical initial conditions and dose budgets.

### Baselines the simulator must beat

1. **Direct statistical mapping.** Regress measured properties (AoR, Hausner ratio) directly on the dosing-fingerprint vector (mass/rev curve, tap mass, afterflow, no-flow fraction) without any simulator. 4. **Nearest-powder carryover.** Use the optimized settings from the most similar previously dosed powder (by fingerprint Euclidean distance). This is the simplest possible transfer baseline.

### When to drop the simulator from the paper

Drop the DEM simulator from the manuscript if any of the following hold:

- **Phase 0 fails:** Synthetic recovery cannot recover ≥3 of 4 parameters within 20%, even after reducing to 3 parameters. This indicates the dosing fingerprint does not contain enough information to identify the DEM parameters, and the calibration is fundamentally ill-posed.

- **Phase 1 fails:** The GP emulator cannot achieve R² > 0.85 on leave-one-out with 48 + 16 = 64 simulations. This suggests the DEM-to-fingerprint mapping is too noisy, non-smooth, or high-dimensional for the available compute budget.

- **Phase 2 fails:** Predicted AoR and Hausner ratio are outside ±5° and ±0.10 for 2 of 3 powders. This means the calibrated DEM parameters do not generalize to independent tests, and the simulator provides no predictive advantage.

- **Phase 3 fails:** The simulator does not beat all three simple baselines on at least one preregistered primary metric. In this case, the dosing fingerprint alone or the existing multi-task GP approach is sufficient, and the simulator adds complexity without value.

In any failure case, the paper can still report the dosing fingerprint methodology, the Bayesian optimization of controller settings, and the multi-task GP across powders — all of which are publishable contributions independent of the simulator. The simulator attempt becomes a reported negative result that strengthens the paper's credibility.

### Total resource commitment

The feasibility test requires 96 DEM simulations (approximately 192 CPU-hours), 3 powders, approximately 45 dosing experiments, and 6 standard-test sets (AoR and bulk/tap density). With one graduate student and AI agents, this can be completed in approximately 2–3 weeks, leaving ample time before the March 2027 conference deadline.

## 8. Summary of Key Numbers

- **DEM cost:** 26–30 CPU-min/rev, approximately 2 CPU-h per full fingerprint evaluation.
- **Emulator training:** 48 simulations (96 CPU-h), with up to 16 adaptive additions.
- **Published calibration budgets:** 60–184 sims for GP (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007); 144 sims for 4 parameters with ACCES/CMA-ES (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041); 34 design points per system with LHS (pqac-00000030).
- **Calibration surface energy reference:** γ = 0.1 mJ/m² for Ti-6Al-4V with Bo = 54.5 (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).
- **Transfer learning savings:** 17–47% R² improvement with 1–5 samples from unseen DEM scenarios; 4–5 iterations to find improved settings with warm-started BO (pqac-00000047).
- **Existing doser baseline:** 42 doses for NaCl (20 screening + 14 optimizer + 8 validation), 0.5 g in 78 s median, 1.8 mg error.
- **Target with simulator:** 20–25 doses per new powder (40–50% reduction).

contexts.context: The excerpt does not establish a universal number of DEM simulations required for a Gaussian-process or polynomial-chaos surrogate. Instead, it reports practical simulation budgets used for MFiX-PIC powder/particle calibration. The deterministic calibration campaign used 60 sampling simulations, while a planned sensitivity study was intended to compare surrogate-based calibration results from 60 versus 120 samples. The Bayesian calibration campaign began with 120 simulations and was augmented by 64 additional factorial-design samples, for a total of 184 simulations. The additional samples were needed because the initial design did not adequately cover the boundaries of the parameter space, leading to posterior distributions peaking at parameter bounds and suggesting potentially large surrogate errors near the edges. Six input parameters were varied in campaign 1, and the quantity of interest was the filling-shock location. Several surrogate types were evaluated, including MARS, linear regression, and Gaussian processes; the Gaussian process model gave one of the best fits, with an unscaled RMSE of 5.188e-03. Thus, the excerpt suggests typical budgets of roughly 60 simulations for an initial deterministic emulator and 120–184 simulations for a more robust Bayesian calibration, but it provides no direct guidance for polynomial-chaos emulators or a general DEM rule.
contexts.question: How many DEM simulations are needed to build a Gaussian process or polynomial chaos surrogate emulator for powder calibration, and what are typical simulation budgets?

contexts.context: The excerpt explains surrogate or metamodel calibration in general, but it does not specify Gaussian-process or polynomial-chaos surrogate construction for powder calibration, nor does it report typical simulation budgets for either method. It does provide useful scaling context: grid-based calibration requires one simulation for every parameter combination and grows exponentially with the number of parameters. A two-parameter, ten-point-per-parameter grid requires 100 simulations, whereas six parameters at ten points each would require one million simulations. For DEM powders, the cited design-of-experiments example calibrated seven microscopic parameters at three levels, implying 3^7 = 2,187 parameter combinations if every combination was evaluated, although the excerpt does not explicitly state the resulting simulation count. The text also cautions that low-order polynomial response surfaces may fail for DEM because contact-parameter effects are highly nonlinear and noisy. Consequently, the passage supports only general observations about surrogate sampling and computational scaling; it does not establish how many simulations are needed for Gaussian-process or polynomial-chaos emulators, nor what budgets are typical in practice.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM framework for calibrating and validating metal powder spreading in additive manufacturing. A Co–Cr powder was characterized experimentally by laser diffraction, with D10, D50, and D90 values of 29.84, 52.08, and 86.11 µm; these particle-size data were converted into the LIGGGHTS particle representation used in simulations. The model was designed for efficient multilayer deposition using approximately 315,000 particles, addressing the limitations of earlier small, single-layer simulations. Calibration and validation relied on experimentally measured static and dynamic angles of repose (AOR), including a measured static AOR of 33°. Spreading tests used a stationary recoater blade and moving stage at 2.54, 5.08, and 12.7 cm/s, while camera images were processed to determine dynamic AOR during deposition. The study links particle and process properties to layer quality through packing density, surface roughness, particle-size distribution, segregation, and AOR. Prior findings summarized in the excerpt indicate that particle cohesion must be included for accurate AOR prediction; increased cohesion and smaller particles reduce packing density and worsen surface roughness. Larger particles increase dynamic AOR and reduce spreadability, while lower translational velocities can improve bed quality. The work also examines particle–recoater interaction and its effect on multilayer powder-bed uniformity.
contexts.question: DEM calibration of metal powder for additive manufacturing spreading, linking particle properties to layer quality and spreadability, validated against experiments

contexts.context: The excerpt provides the methodological basis for calibrating and evaluating a DEM model of metal-powder spreading in laser powder bed fusion, although it does not describe a complete calibration procedure or report quantitative validation results. The model uses particle-level Newtonian force and torque balances, including particle–particle and particle–wall interactions, and is implemented in ESI Group DEM software. The representative material is IN718, with a solid density of 8000 kg/m3. Important contact and damping inputs include sliding and rolling coefficients of 0.1 and 0.7, respectively, plus rolling and twisting damping coefficients of 1.5. Process and geometry parameters include a 0.1 m/s spreader velocity, a 6 × 10−5 m table displacement (layer height), and defined source, build-table, wall, and spreader dimensions. The powder bed is discretized into cells along spreading, build, and transverse directions, enabling spatial analysis of packing and particle distribution. Model outputs include powder density and particle distribution across multiple layers and along the spreading direction. Experimental measurements of packing density and particle-size distribution on the build plate are included for comparison, providing validation targets linked to layer homogeneity and spreadability. Prior findings cited in the excerpt indicate that lower spreader velocity improves bed homogeneity and that blade geometry affects powder-bed quality.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes DEM calibration and validation for powder spreading in laser-powder bed fusion. Because powder is a discrete medium, DEM is commonly used to simulate powder behavior, but its predictions must be experimentally verified. A practical calibration procedure compares DEM-derived flowability measures with experiments, particularly the angle of repose and avalanche angle; apparent density and tap density may also be measured numerically and compared with experimental values. Close agreement is treated as evidence that the DEM model is accurate and can be used to assess related powder-flowability and spreadability behavior. The excerpt links particle and process properties to layer quality through spreadability metrics, including powder-bed density, surface roughness, dynamic repose angle, mass flow rate, powder coverage, spreading throughput, and empty-area fraction. Recoating velocity, layer thickness, particle-size distribution, roller speed, recoater geometry, and recoater type are among the investigated parameters. The motivation is that inadequate spreading produces poor-quality layers and can lead to porosity and unwanted part distortion, whereas high-density, well-spread layers support better fabricated-part performance. The substrate surface roughness is also identified as an important factor in spreadability.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a DEM calibration strategy for powder spreading in selective laser sintering (SLS), relevant to additive-manufacturing powder layer formation and spreadability. Rather than relying only on direct particle-level measurements, the study uses bulk calibration: DEM parameters are varied until simulated bulk behavior matches experimental measurements. The Hertz–Mindlin contact model combined with the JKR adhesion model is selected because SLS particles are assumed not to experience sufficiently high stresses for contact plasticity to be critical. The principal calibrated parameters are interfacial adhesive surface energy and particle–particle rolling friction. Two independent calibration routes are proposed. The first matches the simulated and experimental static angle of repose from powder-heap formation. The second compares experimentally measured unconfined yield strength from shear testing with results from an idealized uniaxial DEM simulation. Each route produces a parameter pair that can reproduce its corresponding experiment; the study then tests whether one common pair can satisfactorily reproduce both sets of results. The associated spreading apparatus permits variation of process conditions, including spreading-tool type and motion, tool gap and shape, and roller rotational velocity. This links particle contact properties and bulk flow behavior to the ability to model layer formation under different spreading configurations, although the excerpt does not report specific metal-powder layer-thickness or surface-quality results.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the powder and process variables most relevant for DEM calibration of metal-powder spreading. Particle size and distribution, shape, composition, internal porosity, and surface morphology are key powder properties; bulk powder behavior is described through flowability and powder-bed density. Spreadability is the principal PBF performance measure because successful recoating should produce uniform layers with adequate laser penetration and improved part quality. Spherical, smooth particles generally improve flowability and packing, while fine particles can increase density but reduce flowability. Non-spherical particles may interlock or entangle, producing non-homogeneous layers that can contribute to porosity. Sieving can narrow the particle-size distribution, remove fines, reduce interparticle cohesion, and improve flowability. The excerpt also provides experimental validation targets for a DEM model: single-layer tests found decreasing powder-bed density as spreading speed increased, stronger sensitivity to layer thickness at higher speeds, and decreasing dimensional accuracy with increasing spreading speed. It cautions that multilayer behavior may differ because melting-induced shrinkage can eventually improve layer thickness and density. These observations support calibrating particle-contact and bulk-flow parameters against measured packing density, layer morphology, thickness uniformity, and speed-dependent spreadability, although specific DEM calibration procedures are not included here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Kennedy–O’Hagan Bayesian calibration framework as a hierarchical statistical model that links noisy physical or experimental observations to potentially biased computer-model outputs. It uses coupled Gaussian-process priors: one represents the simulator response and the other represents systematic discrepancy between simulator predictions and observations, commonly called model error, model-form uncertainty, or structural error. Calibration updates prior distributions for uncertain model parameters using the likelihood of observed outputs, producing posterior distributions rather than a single optimized parameter vector. Bayesian posterior inference jointly uses simulated and field/experimental data to estimate calibration parameters, simulator behavior, and discrepancy-related unknowns. This framework can quantify uncertainty in both calibrated parameters and predicted quantities of interest, while accounting for measurement error and model inadequacy. The key identifiability challenge is separating genuine uncertainty in model input parameters from systematic model bias; both can explain mismatches between simulations and observations, making them difficult to distinguish without informative priors, suitable data, or experimental design. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Kennedy–O’Hagan Bayesian calibration framework as a joint treatment of simulator calibration and model discrepancy. The relationship between observations and the simulator is written as y(x,t) = η(x,t;θ) + δ(x,t) + ε, where η is the MFiX-PIC simulator, θ contains uncertain calibration parameters, δ is a Gaussian-process representation of model-form discrepancy between the simulator and reality, and ε represents observation variability. Calibration begins with prior distributions for θ and Gaussian-process hyperparameters, then uses observations to update these through Bayes’ theorem and obtain a joint posterior. Because the posterior integral is generally intractable, MCMC is used for numerical inference. The framework can estimate parameter uncertainty, account for systematic CFD bias, construct a statistical surrogate or emulator, and propagate parameter, model-form, numerical, and measurement uncertainties to quantities of interest. In this application, an analytical solution rather than experimental data guided calibration, and artificial uncertainty below 1% was introduced to represent experimental uncertainty. The excerpt does not specifically explain discrepancy–parameter identifiability or a synthetic-recovery experiment; it only establishes the model structure through which those issues would arise, since both calibration parameters and discrepancy are inferred from the same observations.
